story: On July 19, 1545, King Henry VIII watched in horror from Southsea Castle as his favorite warship, the Mary Rose, suddenly sank during the Battle of the Solent. The mighty carrack had just fired her guns and was turning to bring her other broadside to bear when a sudden gust of wind caught her sails. She heeled over, and water rushed into her lower gunports, which had been left open after firing. The ship plunged to the seabed in minutes. Anti-boarding netting trapped most of the crew below, resulting in the loss of roughly 500 men, with fewer than 35 surviving. Rediscovered centuries later, the remarkably preserved wreck and its 19,000 artefacts now survive as a stunning Tudor time capsule.
angle: King Henry VIII watched in horror from shore as his favorite warship capsized and sank in minutes, taking nearly 500 men down with her.

claims.claim: The Mary Rose sank on 19 July 1545 during the Battle of the Solent.

evidence.quote: After being substantially rebuilt in 1536, she saw her last action on 19 July 1545.
1545 - On 19 July, at the Battle of the Solent, the ship sinks while leading the attack on the French invasion fleet.
The Mary Rose sank on 19th July 1545 while leading the attack against a huge French invasion fleet, much larger than that of the Spanish Armada forty-three years later.

claims.claim: King Henry VIII watched the sinking from Southsea Castle.

evidence.quote: Legend has it that Henry VIII watched in horror from Southsea castle along with the wife of Vice Admiral Sir George Carew.
The air was hot and still as Henry VIII stood on the walls of Southsea Castle on 19 July 1545, looking out over the Solent.

claims.claim: A survivor testified that the ship heeled over in the wind while turning and water entered through open gunports.

evidence.quote: According to the unnamed Fleming, the ship had fired all of her guns on one side and was turning to present the guns on the other side to the enemy ship, when she was caught in a strong gust of wind, heeled and took in water through the open gunports.

Accounts on what happened that day differ, but one survivor claimed the ship had just fired its guns on one side and was turning to fire from the other when the wind caught its sails and plunged the open gunports below the water, which sank it.
...who stated that the Mary Rose 'heeled over with the wind' and that 'water entered by the lowest row of gun ports which had been left open after firing'.

claims.claim: Anti-boarding netting on the upper decks trapped many men as the ship went down.

evidence.quote: What turned the sinking into a major tragedy was the anti-boarding netting that covered the upper decks in the waist (the midsection of the ship) and the sterncastle.
Only 35 men survived disaster, according to contemporary records. Many would have been trapped under the anti-boarding netting and drowned.

claims.claim: The wreck of the Mary Rose was raised from the seabed in 1982.

evidence.quote: The wreck of the Mary Rose was located in 1971 and was raised on 11 October 1982 by the Mary Rose Trust in one of the most complex and expensive maritime salvage projects in history.
The Mary Rose was raised from the seabed of the Solent in 1982, and has been on display before, but it is only now that insights into life on board are being shown to the public.
The lasting legacy from the battle, the Mary Rose, was raised from the Solent seabed in 1982 and is now on display at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard.

claims.claim: Vice Admiral Sir George Carew went down with the ship.

evidence.quote: The only positively identified person who went down with the ship was Vice-Admiral George Carew.
Only the names of the vice admiral, Sir George Carew, and the master, Roger Grenville, are known.
...and the ship’s captain, Vice Admiral George Carew, was a favourite of Henry’s – they had even dined together the night before.

claims.claim: The Mary Rose was ordered by King Henry VIII and built in Portsmouth starting in 1510.

evidence.quote: Construction of Mary Rose began on 29 January 1510 in Portsmouth and she was launched in July 1511.
1510 - The ship is ordered by the newly crowned King Henry VIII and construction begins in Portsmouth. It is launched in 1511.

claims.claim: The French invasion fleet was led by Admiral Claude d'Annebault.

evidence.quote: The French expedition started disastrously, with the 800-ton flagship Philippe or Carraquon being destroyed on 6 July in an accidental fire while at anchor in the Seine. Admiral Claude d'Annebault transferred his flag to La Maistresse...
In May 1545, the French assembled a large fleet in the estuary of the River Seine and on 16th July the huge French force under the command of Admiral Claude d’Annebault set sail for England.

claims.claim: French historians or officers claimed that French gunfire sank the Mary Rose.

evidence.quote: Contrary to all other accounts, Martin du Bellay, a French cavalry officer who was present at the battle, stated that the Mary Rose had been sunk by French guns.
French historians claim its forces were responsible for sinking the Mary Rose in battle.

disputed: The exact cause of the sinking: while a survivor's account and contemporary records point to open gunports and a strong gust of wind causing the ship to take on water during a turn, a contemporary French account claimed French gunfire sank her, and modern theories also suggest overloading, top-heaviness from modifications, crew insubordination, or an epidemic of dysentery. A script should present the survivor's open-gunport account as eyewitness testimony while attributing the French claim to French historians.

The number of men aboard: contemporary records and estimates state roughly 400 to 500 men, while later family accounts (such as the Carew biography) claim 700 men were on board. A script should use approximately 500 men as supported by provisions and crew lists.
